topic: AI Agent Architecture Tutorial: A 20-Chapter Guide to Designing and Building Production AI Agents

competitors.title: Building Effective Agents (Anthropic)
key_points: Establishes the foundational mental model: start with the simplest solution and only add complexity when needed; often the best architecture is not agentic at all
Introduces the augmented LLM as the basic building block: an LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools, and memory via the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
Defines five key workflow patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (sectioning + voting), orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer
Distinguishes workflows (predictable, well-defined tasks) from agents (flexible, model-driven decision-making at scale)
Agents are typically 'just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop', with stopping conditions and human checkpoints for control
Recommends testing in sandboxed environments and designing toolsets/documentation carefully, given higher cost and compounding-error risk

competitors.title: A Practical Guide to Building Agents (OpenAI)
key_points: Defines an agent as 'systems that independently accomplish tasks on your behalf', contrasting with workflows and single-turn LLM apps
Agent core components: (1) the LLM powering reasoning and decisions, (2) tools/APIs for action, (3) explicit guidelines and guardrails defining behavior
Identifies when to build agents: complex decision-making, difficult-to-maintain rules, and heavy reliance on unstructured data
Introduces orchestration patterns: single-agent systems (a model with tools executing a loop until an exit condition) versus multi-agent systems
Manager pattern: a central LLM orchestrates specialized agents via tool calls and handoffs, keeping context and control centralized
Recommends maximizing a single agent's capabilities first; only split into multiple agents when prompts get too complex or tool selection fails
Covers guardrails, hooks, and prompt templates with policy variables to reduce maintenance burden

competitors.title: What is an AI agent? (LangChain)
key_points: Explains how agents work in an LLM loop: the model repeatedly reasons, acts via tools, observes results, and iterates
Distinguishes agents from plain workflows, emphasizing reliability and production readiness for autonomous systems
Positions agent architecture as combining a model, tools, and a runtime loop that manages state, planning, and action selection
Frames the practical question of where workflows fit versus autonomous agents for building reliable systems

competitors.title: How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)
key_points: Multi-agent architecture with a lead agent orchestrating parallel subagents excels at breadth-first research tasks
Internal eval: a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 lead + Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval
Token usage explains 80% of performance variance (with tool calls and model choice the other two factors) — multi-agent distributes work across separate context windows to add parallel capacity
Separate context windows prevent context pollution and enable parallel reasoning across independent directions
Recommends a lead-agent model that can synthesize and a set of focused subagents for parallel independent subtasks

competitors.title: Agentic systems overview (Anthropic Docs)
key_points: Provides an architectural decision framework for choosing between simple workflows and autonomous agents based on task predictability
Details tool use, memory, and context management as the core augmentations that make agents effective
Emphasizes design principles for production agents: clear stopping conditions, guardrails, sandboxing, and observability

stats.fact: Anthropic found that multi-agent research systems with a lead agent and parallel subagents outperformed a single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on its internal research eval.
In Anthropic's analysis, token usage alone explains 80% of performance variance on the BrowseComp evaluation, with number of tool calls and model choice as the other two factors (together 95%).

Anthropic's Building Effective Agents guide defines five core workflow patterns — prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer — plus the autonomous agent as the final escalation.
Anthropic recommends using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to integrate a growing ecosystem of third-party tools with a simple client implementation for augmenting the base LLM.
OpenAI defines an agent as 'a system that independently accomplishes tasks on your behalf' and says applications that don't use the LLM to control workflow execution are not agents.
stats.source: OpenAI: A Practical Guide to Building Agents

stats.fact: OpenAI's agent core components are the LLM, tools (external functions/APIs), and explicit guidelines and guardrails; orchestration falls into single-agent vs multi-agent (manager) patterns.
stats.source: OpenAI: A Practical Guide to Building Agents

stats.fact: OpenAI recommends maximizing a single agent's capabilities by incrementally adding tools before splitting into a multi-agent system, to keep complexity and evaluation manageable.
stats.source: OpenAI: A Practical Guide to Building Agents

angles: Workflow-first: how to decide when a simple prompt chain or a fixed workflow is better than a fully autonomous agent — and avoid over-engineering
The augmented LLM as the core unit: model + tools + memory + retrieval, assembled with MCP instead of custom integrations
Pattern-driven design: applying the five Anthropic workflows (chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) to real problems
Single-agent vs multi-agent: the practical threshold for splitting, plus the manager/orchestrator-worker patterns
Context and memory as first-class architecture concerns: separate context windows, short-term vs long-term memory, and preventing context pollution
Guardrails, safety, and control in production: stopping conditions, human checkpoints, sandboxing, and observability
The economics of agents: token usage as the dominant performance/cost lever, and how architecture scales it
Building vs frameworks: when to use Agents SDK / LangChain / Claude Agent SDK vs hand-rolling the loop

Chapter 2: The agent loop — reasoning, acting, observing, and exit conditions
Chapter 3: Core components — the model, tools, guardrails, and hooks

Chapter 5: Prompt chaining workflow
Chapter 6: Routing workflow
Chapter 7: Parallelization — sectioning and voting
Chapter 8: Orchestrator-workers pattern
Chapter 9: Evaluator-optimizer pattern
Chapter 10: The autonomous agent pattern
Chapter 11: Single-agent architecture — adding tools incrementally and prompt templates
Chapter 12: Multi-agent architecture — manager and decentralized handoff patterns
Chapter 13: Memory and context management (short-term, long-term, context windows)
Chapter 14: Tool design and integration via MCP
Chapter 15: Guardrails, safety, and control — stopping conditions and human checkpoints
Chapter 16: Observability and evaluation of agentic systems
Chapter 17: Cost management and token-budget economics
Chapter 18: Frameworks and SDKs — Agents SDK, LangChain, Claude Agent SDK, vs hand-rolling

Chapter 20: Production checklist and decision framework for choosing your architecture
Conclusion: Putting it together and where to go next
